chunks: From him, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, from Hafs ibn Suqah and 'Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from Zurarah, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'What is the thing for which there is no expiation (kaffarah) for breaking a vow?' He said: 'Whatever brings you benefit in your religion or worldly affairs, there is no expiation for breaking a vow regarding it.'

key_terms.حِنْثَ: Breaking of a vow, requiring expiation
key_terms.نَذْرَ: Vow or pledge to perform an act

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on breaking a vow for a beneficial act in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that vows concerning beneficial acts in religion or worldly life do not incur expiation (*kaffarah*) if broken, distinguishing them from obligatory vows. This ruling reflects the Shia juristic principle that a vow to perform a recommended or neutral act does not elevate it to a binding obligation requiring penalty for omission. The narration underscores the flexibility in personal vows (*nadhr*) when the subject matter is inherently beneficial rather than strictly obligatory.
